rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.5 and Tables 1-3 - the study runs its own EPANET/Monte Carlo simulations (OPTIEN) of the Fuente Palmera on-demand network using 2007 flow data recorded at the pumping station, and reports pressures, power and energy savings (up to ~27%) for four management scenarios.
rows.notes: The study's own results concern energy requirements and energy savings of on-demand pressurised networks under sectoring and dynamic pressure regulation; it reports nothing of its own on water losses, conveyance efficiency or water conservation. The statements that conveyance efficiency rises from 60-70% to near 100% and that on-demand supply allows more efficient on-farm systems and cuts water use by up to 50% appear only in the Introduction and are attributed to Rodriguez Diaz et al. (2008), so they do not count as own evidence. The simulation is not compared with measured energy or water data either. Q2 therefore 'no'.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.5 and Tables 1-3 - own simulation runs (EPANET engine, 1500 Monte Carlo iterations per open-hydrant probability) of the Fuente Palmera irrigation district network, with energy savings reported per scenario.
rows.notes: The study does not test drip or micro-irrigation at all; it is a hydraulic/energy simulation of a pressurised distribution network at district level. The only mention of trickle/sprinkler systems is an introductory remark that pressurised networks enable their use, which is not a result. No own evidence on drip water conservation.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a modelling paper on energy (not water) in on-demand pressurised networks; the water-conservation and conveyance-efficiency statements the review attributes to it are cited from earlier work in the Introduction.
